The company offers a ticket inventory for over 1.8 lakh bus routes across India, operated by more than 700 bus operators. The company sold around 40-50 lakh tickets during the financial year 2012. It sold more than $10^{\wedge 0}$ lakh seats and has recorded a registered consumer base of 20 lakh, reporting an average growth rate of 250 per cent during the last five years. The company was founded in 2006 by Phanindra Sama, Charan Padmaraju, and Sudhakar Pasupunuri, who were classmates from BITS Pilani. All the three founders who used to work in Bangalore with top IT MNCs such as IBM, Texas Instruments, and Honeywell quit their well-paying, secure jobs to found Redbus. During the Diwali season of 2005, Phanindra Sama wanted to spend the festival in his home town (HSS-362) Page 2 of 3 but was not able to buy a ticket. He never made it home and that was the beginning of Redbus. Phanindra realized the need for a system, which could be used by bus operators to display their seats and remove middlemen from the ticket reservation process. He decided to bring to those traveling by buses the same convenience that consumers enjoy while booking air tickets online. Once Phanindra and his two co-founders felt that they understood the business, they developed a plan and submitted it to the TiE, Bangalore chapter (the Indus Entrepreneurs) mentorship competition. They were among the three winners. The initial seed funding and mentoring was provided by TiE and the founders also made personal investments to launch their portal and service. Redbus has raised more than USD 75 lakh from three round of funding. In 2007, the company raised USD 10 lakh in angel funding from Seedfund, an early-stage investor. In 2009, the company received an undisclosed second round funding from Inventus Capital Partners and Seedfund. Again, during May 2011, Redbus raised USD 65 lakh from Helion Venture Partners, Inventus Capital Partners, and Seedfund in its Series $C$ funding. Today, In the present time, the customer can book return tickets, get standard fares, and comprehensive information from a single source. Travel agents can bill more by offering return tickets and get access to all bus operators instead of only a handful. Bus operators realize their payments on that day the customer travels unlike the 3-4 weeks it took earlier. Updates are available on extra buses during festive occasions. Redbus is looking for business expansion and is in talks with few offline bus ticketing companies in Singapore and Malaysia. Questions:

questions.question: Raju works as a Medical Representative for the city branch of a leading pharmaceutical company. He is hard working and has a very pleasing personality that impresses most of the doctors and customers that he meets. The company set the monthly targets for each medical representative in terms of the number of new customers and the total volume of sales to be achieved. Representatives who achieve the monthly targets are eligible for the special sales incentives, the only lucrative monetary benefit offered by the company. Raju was lagging behind his targets for the past seven months. Although Raju has achieved 97% of the target set this month, he knew that he would cut a sorry figure and the Regional Manager would not take him at face value. The last time round he had committed to the Regional Manager that he would ensure that the targets were met. Mr. Pradeep Jain, Regional Manager, liked to be in total control of any situation. He considered himself to be very knowledgeable and does not entertain suggestions and ideas from his team members. He believed in issuing instructions to the subordinates and expected them to follow his instructions. He kept an eye on the performance of his 12-member team of sales representatives throughout the twelve- odd hours that they work. He expected his team members to keep him informed about their progress on any target on an hourly basis even when they were on the field. The targets, in terms of the volumes and number of contacts were scaled up consistently and were so high that achieving them seemed a difficult task. After mailing the monthly reports, Raju went into Pradeep Jain’s room only to be given a strong warning that if the achievement of targets for the month ahead was also below expectations, it would cost him his job. Most of his colleagues too had a similar experience to narrate after they had submitted their monthly report. Page 1 of 4 The next day Pradeep Jain called for a meeting, where he described in detail how he had worked when he was in their position such as carrying as many medical flashcards of the new products as possible and carrying most of the samples and so forth. questions.subject: local:essentials-of-management-engineering-economics
questions.question: Case Study: Daewoo was founded in 1967 by its hardworking, relentlessly driven chairman Kim Woo-Choong. After its initial success in exporting textiles, the company expanded into trade, autos, machinery, consumer electronics, construction, heavy shipping, computers, telephones, and financial services, becoming Korea's fourth largest business group. It became a textile supplier for Sears, Christian Dior, Calvin Klein, and London Fog. It also engaged in a joint venture with General Motors (GM) to build the Le Mans car. However, labor and other problems limited car shipments. Chairman Kim's philosophy of hard work and the value placed in people were important factors in the firm's success. However, in the late $1980s$ and early $1990s$, the company faced several problems. For one, Kim was concerned that, with the increasing prosperity of Koreans, the work force might lose the spirit of hard work. Moreover, there was growing discontent among younger workers and decreasing motivation. Through Kim's hands-off approach to managing, some of the companies in the Daewoo group went out of control. For example, in the unprofitable heavy shipping unit, he noticed many unnecessary expenses. The elimination of company-sponsored barbershops saved the company \$8 million a year. In general, Daewoo's work force (HSS-302) Page 1 of 5 was young and well educated. In contrast to similar positions in many other Korean companies, top positions at Daewoo were occupied by managers with no family ties. Although Daewoo was a major company with its 91,000 employees, it was not dominant in any one industry. The strategy of being a supplier for major companies, such as Caterpillar, GM, and Boeing, may have led to opportunities being bypassed for becoming a major marketer of its own brands. Now in the $1990s, Kim$ was also looking at opportunities in Europe; for example, he formed a joint venture with a distribution company in France. The massive restructuring had already shown some positive effects. Kim sold some steel, financial, and real estate units. The hands-off managerial style had been replaced by a hands-on style, resulting in re-centralization. Managers were “retired” or otherwise let go. Thousands of positions were also eliminated. Things were looking better in 1991. The company lost money in 1988 and 1989 but made some profit in 1990 partly because of the sale of some major assets. The joint venture with GM registered a healthy growth. The company was also optimistic about the future of the new compact car Espero. Still, Daewoo had to cope with its labor costs and Japanese competition. What looked good in the early $1990s$ dramatically changed in the latter part of that decade and especially in the years 2000 to 2002. In 2000, Ford planned to buy Daewoo Motor for some \$7billion. However, the deal fell apart later that year. Moreover, the company went bankrupt in November 2000. Chairman Kim mysteriously disappeared. He liked to think big, and he also left behind the company with big debts. Several billion dollars were also unaccounted for. With Ford out of the picture, GM entered seriously into negotiations with Daewoo, which was once Korea’s second biggest car maker. On April 30, 2002, GM agreed to buy the bankrupt company, which was renamed as GM-Daewoo. What is in it if for GM? The acquisition is a key component of its global strategy. On the other hand, restructuring Daewoo is going to be a formidable task. The brand image has to be restored and the Korean market share of 10 percent (which was 37 percent in 1998) has to be improved. The product line also has to be reviewed and complemented with new models. Moreover, GM- Daewoo can expect difficulties with Korea’s aggressive unions. Questions: i. What are the advantages and disadvantages of hands-off, decentralized (02) management approach? ii. What were some of the controllable and uncontrollable factors in this case? How (03) should Mr. Kim have responded to those factors? iii. How can Daewoo stay competitive with the Japanese? (02) (HSS-302) Page 2 of 5

Values are exchanged if lower numbered processor contains the larger value. 1 ½ Mark Below is the example gives such sorting of 8 values on one-dimensional mesh processor model: Indices: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 (CSE 607) 8 Page of 2 Initial 7 8 6 4 5 3 2 1 Values: After < < < ___ Odd-even 7 6 8 4 5 2 3 1 | Exchange $|1^{st}$ iter < < < < | Even-odd 6 7 4 8 2 5 1 3 ___ | exchange After < < < ___ Odd-even 6 4 7 2 8 1 5 3 | Exchange $|2^{nd}$ iter < < < < | Even-odd 4 6 2 7 1 8 3 5 ___ | exchange After < < < ___ Odd-even 4 2 6 1 7 3 8 5 | Exchange $|3^{rd}$ iter < < < < | Even-odd 2 4 1 6 3 7 5 8 ___ | exchange After < < < ___ Odd-even 2 1 4 3 6 5 7 8 | Exchange $|4^{th}$ iter < < < < | Even-odd 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ___ | Exchange 1 ½ MArks Odd-even transposition sort(one dimensional mesh processor array): Parameter n Global i Local $a,t \{$ For$(i=1;i\le n/2;i++)$ For all $P$_{j }, where $0\le j\le n-1$ do { If $j<(n-1)$ and $odd(j)$ then $\{ t\leftarrow$successor(a); successor$(a)\leftarrow \max (a,t); a \leftarrow \min (a,t); \}$ If even$(j)$ then (CSE 607) 9 Page of 2 $\{ t\leftarrow$successor(a); successor$(a)\leftarrow \max (a,t); a \leftarrow \min (a,t); \} \} 2$ Marks } Here $n/2$ iterations are sufficient to sort n elements and llel algorithm has $O(n)$ as time complexity.

After making preliminary enquiries he writes a letter to the Project Manager enquiring the reasons for delay and asking for the proposed date of completion of the project. He also states that the Finance Executive needs to be informed of the delay and it is better to meet the Finance Executive in person. Mr. Taylor feels that Mr. Kiran has not answered his queries properly. Further, he could not understand why he needs to meet the Finance Executive. He feels that Kiran is avoiding the responsibility. Taylor summons Kiran and tells him to get the work done immediately and asks Kiran if he faces any specific problems in getting the work done, for which Kiran shakes his head and promises to do his best. questions.question: Your organization has a contract with a firm outside India. As a team leader you have signed a contract related one of the joint- programs planned in India. A month before the program you wrote to the coordinator of the firm related to some changes required. The coordinator seemed not very happy and expressed the view that such re-negotiations on already planned work is not encouraged. The coordinator seems to represent: • Individualism • Masculinity • Particularism • Universalism 2 $10^3 17, 18$ 3 Analyse the following case using $G$ Hofstede’s notions of cultural dimensions (500-600 words) Sara worked in a clothing boutique in Finland (Auralines) that ordered clothes from India, mainly from Bangalore. The Finnish Company ordered clothes from India in advance and clearly mentioned the required date of delivery and expected that the goods will be delivered on time. The Indian firm Blinddots Pvt. Ltd. responded enthusiastically and provided all the details related to the products to Sara and her colleague who were asked to coordinate from the Finnish side. The manager from the Indian firm agreed to the possibility of sending the order before the scheduled time and even offered to send a few samples in addition to the ordered items. The Manager from Auralines instructed Sara and her colleague to make sure that the orders are in place and all the agreements related to the deadlines, due dates of the payments and delivery dates are confirmed with the manufacturer once again. Sara contacted the Indian side over the phone and they assured that there need not be any anxiety on this. However, when the delivery date came, no goods were delivered or even sent from India. The Finnish team received a mail from the Indian manager stating due to certain unforeseen event the goods could not be sent, but every effort would be made to send the goods within twenty days. The manager in Finland blamed the Sara and her colleague for not doing their task well and contacted the people in India directly. He asked for a meeting with the Indian team on reaching Bangalore to resolve the issue. The Finnish manager wanted to go straight to Business and talk about the orders when the Indians wanted to have a dinner and take the time for get together first. The Indian manager informed that his team was keen on the project and viewed it as an honour to the company. However, the Finnish manager, found the members of Indian team rude as they came physically very close in the meetings and did not stick to the point. Also he noticed that the Indians were too respectful towards him than to his colleagues and tried to please him with their pleasantries. He could not understand why the leader of the Indian team kept repeating about the problems related to HR in his firm and could not identify the people responsible for the delay. When the Finnish manager enquired about the possibility of maintaining the deadline for delivery in future, he got a positive response. At the same time, the Indian manager gave him vague answers related to the scheduled delivery though everything seemed ready. The Indian team members felt that the Finnish manager was too reserved. He was not interested in the people talking to him but focused only on getting the business done. In addition, they felt amused that his employees were talking to him casually without any formality. Despite Indians hinting that the work is in progress related to delivery and there would be a slight delay due to some HR reasons, the Finnish manager refused to see their commitment. They felt the Manager was trying to hide his incompetence as a leader by being insistent on time. The entire situation turned to the worse and the two teams closed the meeting without any solutions. 2 Analyse the following case using concepts of non-verbal $10^5 11, 17$ 4 communication across cultures (200-300 words) An American supervisor in a multinational firm calls in the Japanese employee for an annual evaluation. questions.subject: local:information-storage-and-management
questions.question: Application Programming Interface (API) Application Programming Interface (API) -A high level implementation that specifies how clients can make service requests. -A set of function calls that enables communication. Binary large object (BLOB) -The actual data without the descriptive info. The user data represents the actual content of a file and is independent of the filename and physical location. C-Clip -A package containing the user's data and associated metadata C-Clip ID (C-Clip handle or C-Clip reference) is the CA that the system returns to the client application. Content Address (CA) -Hash algorithm creates the content address/ object address. -Hash algo considers all aspects of the content while generating CA to the user application. A unique number is calculated from the sequence of bits of the file content. -An identifier that uniquely addresses the content of a file and not its location. Unlike location-based addresses, content addresses are inherently stable and, once calculated, they never change and always refer to the same content. -The hash output or digest is a type of fingerprint and is used to locate the file in CAS. -When a user tries to retrieve a file, server sends the CA to CAS with appropriate fn to read the file. CAS uses CA to locate the file and passes it back to the application server. C-Clip Descriptor File (CDF) An XML file that the system creates when making a C-Clip. This file includes the CAs or all referenced BLOBs and associated metadata. Metadata includes characteristics of CAS objects such as size, format and expiry date. 2 Marks Client present the data to be archived to the CAS API. The application server may also interact directly with the source like X-ray $m/c API$ seperates the BLOB from the from meta data and CA is calculated from object’s binary representation. CA and metadata of the object are then inserted into the C-Clip DF. The C-Clip is then transferred to CAS. 3 Marks

questions.subject: local:information-storage-and-management
questions.question: Backup server init request to backup client. Backup server init request to backup client. This request instructs the backup client to send its metadata to backup server and the data to be backed up to the appropriate storage node. On receiving this request, backup client sends the metadata to the backup server. Backup server writes this metadata on its metadata catalog. Backup client also sends the data to the storage node and storage node writes the data to the storage device. After all the data is backed up, the storage node closes the connection to the backup device. Backup server writes backup completion status to the metadata catalog. Backup $s/w$ provides reporting capabilities based on backup catalog and $\log$ files. They include info such as amount of data backed up, no. of completed backups, no. of incompleted backups, types of errors while backing etc. 2 Marks 2 Marks .Physical Tape library: -Provides housing and power for a no of tape drives and tape cartridges along with robotic arm (Picker mech.).Backup $s/w$ has intelligence to manage the robotic arm and entire backup process. -Tape drives RD/WR data from and to a tape. -Tape cartridges are placed in the slots when not in use. -Robotic arms are used move tapes around the library. -Each physical component in a tape library has an individual element address, used as an addressing mechanism. -It is necessary to ensure that the tape drive is kept busy continuously to prevent the gaps between the blocks. -Gaps can be eliminated by buffering the data on the tape drive or by adjusting speed of the tape drive to match data transfer rate. 1 Mark

questions.question: Little’$s Law$: Describes the relationship between the number of requests in a queue and the response time. $N = a \times R$ “$N$” is the total number of requests in the queuing system “a” is the arrival rate “$R$” is the average response time (or TAT i.e. time from arrival to departure from system) Utilization law: Defines the $I/O$ controller utilization $U = a \times Rs$ “$U$” is the $I/O$ controller utilization 2 Marks “RS“ is the service time Arrival 6 5 4 3 2 $1^{I/}$ ControllerO black box: consisting of two elements: Queue: Loc. where the $I/O$ requests wait before it is processed by the $I/O$ controller. Disk $I/O$ controller: Processes I/Os that are waiting in the queue one by one. Arrival rate: Rate at which $I/O$ requests arrive at the controller (Generated by the application) Arrival rate, queue length and time taken by the $I/O$ controller to process each request $\det$ the performance of the disk system. Utilization of $I/O$ controller $(U= a \times Rs)$ Total response time $(R=R$_{s}$/1-U)$ But $R$_{a}$=1/a U=R$_{s}$/R$_{a} $S=$service rate-arrival rate And $R = 1/ ($service rate-arrival rate) On simplifying Hence Average response time $= R= R$_{s} $/ (1-U)$ Number of requests in a queue $N$_{Q} = Number requests in the system $N -$Number od requests on the controller $N$_{Q} $= N - U = a X R - U = aX (R$_{s} $/(1-U)) - U$ On simplifying Average queue size $= U^{2} / (1-U)$ Time spent by a request in the queue = time spent by a request in the system OR $avg$ response time - the time spent on the controller $= R$_{s} $/ (1-U) - R$_{s} On simplifying Time spent by a request in the queue $= U x R$ 3 Marks 2A. HOT SPARE refers to a spare HDD in a RAID set that temporarily replaces a failed HDD of a RAID set. Hot spare takes the identity of the failed HDD in the array. Methods of data recovery depending on RAID impl: -If parity RAID is used, then the data is rebuilt onto the hot spare from the parity and the data on the surviving HDDs in the surviving set. -If mirroring is used, then the data from the surviving mirror is used to copy the data. When failed HDD is replaced with a new HDD, one of the following takes place: -Hot spare replaces new HDD permanently. i.e. it is no longer a hot spare, and a new hot spare is added to the array. -When a new HDD is added to the system, data from the hot spare is copied to it. The hot spare returns to its idle state, ready to replace the next failed drive. 2 Marks DISK LOAD IN RAID $5: =0.6 \times 5,200+4x(0.4 \times 5,200) [B,ze$ the write penalty for RAID 5 is 4] =11,440 IOPS DISK LOAD IN RAID $1: =0.6 \times 5,200+2x(0.4 \times 5,200) [B,ze$ the write penalty for RAID 1 is 2] =7,280 IOPS 2 Marks The computed diskload determines the no of disk required for application. If an HDD with a specification of a maximum 180 IOPS for the application, the no of disks required to meet the workload for the RAID will be RAID5: 11,440 / 180 = 64 disks RAID 1: 7,280 / 180 = 42 disks (Nearest Even no.) 1 Marks

questions.question: Cache vaulting Cache is exposed to the risk of uncommitted data loss due to power failure. To solve problem: Powering the memory $\ldots$.. In the event of extended power failure, large amount of data may not be committed HENCE, STORAGE VENDORS USE A SET OF PHYSICAL DISKS TO DUMP THE CONTENTS OF CACHE DURING POWER FAILURE. THIS IS CALLED CACHE VAULTING AND DISK DRIVES ARE CALLED VAULT DRIVES. Powering the memory with a battery until AC power is restored OR using the battery power to write the cache content to the disk. As power is restored, data from these disks is written back to the write cache and then written to the intended disk. 3 Marks Physical drives are logically split into volumes known as logical volumes, referred as LOGICAL VOLUME NUMBERs (LUNs). -LUN improves disk utilization. LUN masking is access control mechanism LUN masking is a process that provides data access control by defining which LUNs a host can access. (08) Ben is a successful Purchasing Manager with a reputation for being hard working and fair. In his regular Monday morning team meeting, the participants are Harry, Charlie, Jim and Sally; Ben gets along with them all and takes their ideas on how to proceed further. The members are free to express any novel techniques employed by them to achieve the goals. After the latest meeting, Ben is surprised when Sally approaches him and complains, "Ben, you have a prejudice against women. First thing in today's meeting, I suggested we consolidate the commodity purchasing into one section, before I was halfway through, you cut in to let Jim speak. By the end of the meeting, you agreed with my idea, but gave Jim all the credit." Ben doesn't know what to think, and besides, he can't even remember Sally bringing up the idea in the first place. "Is something wrong with Sally today?," he wonders, "Why is she making a federal case out of this? This is the problem when you let women take up men’s work. They always make everything an emotional issue." So he makes a joke to minimize the situation, “ Don’t worry Sally, next month I will go for all new ideas and you will lead the team , I promise.’’ Sally gets annoyed and replies, “I am not bothered about what you will do next month. I am not even sure whether I should continue if it goes like this. All I want is to let you know that I am hurt by the way I was treated in the meeting.” Page 3 of 4 $V$. He has been working closely with Naina, the Indian team leader, to develop a new networking program. While reviewing his work from the previous week, Michael discovers that he made a mistake in the programming code. He notices that Naina corrected his error, but wonders why Naina did not bring it to his attention so that he could avoid delays and keep from making the same mistake in the future. He asked Naina to meet him in his office to discuss the issue. Naina entered office with a smile on her face and greeted him politely. However, when Michael brought the issue of correction, she began to look sideways and avoided his glance. She apologized for correcting the error and did not explain the reasons for it. Michael stared at her expecting Naina to argue with him over the error. Naina began to feel uneasy and looked down at the floor. Michael felt that she is hiding something from him and got irritated. • How might this behavior be explained? What do you think is taking place? VI. Analyze the following case on the basis of your understanding of Edward Hall’s theory of communication styles: (07) Mr. Brian, an American, has just joined as the Head of Operations of the Indian Branch of a large multinational firm. While reviewing the projects currently being implemented, he notices a big problem with one of them. This particular project is running way behind schedule and there have also been large over-runs in terms of cost. After making preliminary enquiries he writes a letter to the Project Manager enquiring the reasons for delay and asking for the proposed date of completionof the project. The Project Manager Mr. Sathish knew that there was a problem in completion of the project due to some pending permissions. The permissions needed to be cleared by the Finance Executive, but the Finance Executive was keeping them on hold as he did not have good relations with the earlier Head of Operations of the firm. Mr. Sathish sends a letter to Mr. Brian stating that he was sorry for the delay but would try his best to overcome such problems in future. He also states that the Finance Executive needs to be informed of the delay and it is better to meet the Finance Executive in person. Mr. Brian feels that Mr. Sathish has not answered his queries properly as he has given no reasons for the delay and not specified the proposed date of completion. Further, he could not understand why he needs to meet the Finance Executive. He feels that Satish is avoiding the responsibility. Brian summons Sathish and tells him to get the work done immediately. Sathish looks down and nods his head. Brian asks Sathish if he faces any specific problems in getting the work done, for which Sathish shakes his head and promises to do his best. Brian seems puzzled as Sathish walks out of the room silently without submitting any concrete plans. He feels that Sathish does not want to work under him for some reasons. Questions: • What are the reasons for miscommunication? • What are your suggestions to avoid such miscommunication in future? IV. (08) A team of managers is meeting to set up a new project team. One of the people being considered is a woman and one of the men says that he heard that the woman being considered was pregnant. The team leader, Mr. Stevan, is of the opinion that the woman in question is a competent person and her inputs may enhance the efficiency, and help them to get better results. Yet, he wants to take a decision on this based on the majority view and asks the members to express their views. One of the members, Mr. Paul stated that because the project was very time-sensitive, he saw no point in involving the woman as it may affect their performance if she is not able to give Page 3 of 4 her time later. A number of male managers seem to agree with the opinion and feel that they may not able to complete the target if there is a change in the team halfway through. Ms. Reema, a female member is of the view that as the immediate monetary incentives completely depends on the quality of the project, they should think carefully before taking any risk. Overall, the members feel that the team leader should consider the completion of the project in a successful way as a priority. $V$. The supervisor concludes that the employee is not happy with the feedback. When the supervisor tries to draw it out of him, the employee continues to smile. questions.question: The abstract of an article entitled ‘A new CubeSat design with 2 3 1, 1, 3 reconfigurable multi-band radios for dynamic spectrum satellite 2, 2, communication networks’ authored by $Ian F$. Jornet, Shuai Nie and published in the Elsevier journal on Ad Hoc 3, 3 Networks, Volume 86, 1 April 2019, Pages 166-178, is given below. 4 Produce a write-up on your understanding of their research findings. ABSTRACT Small satellites, or CubeSats, are envisioned as a promising solution for future satellite communication networks because of their low costs and short deployment cycle. Currently, CubeSats communicate at conventionally allocated satellite communication frequencies. However, with the increase in the number of CubeSats, CubeSat- enabled communication systems, and many new use cases, new spectrum bands and a more efficient spectrum usage are needed. In this paper, a novel CubeSat design with reconfigurable multi-band radios for communication in dynamic frequencies is proposed. The multi-band radio design is realized by two complementary approaches, namely, an electronics-based and a photonics-based approach. The multi-band communication covers a wide range from radio frequencies (2-30 GHz), millimeter wave (30- 300 GHz), Terahertz band (up to 10 THz), and optical frequencies (with typical bands of 850 nm/350 THz, 1300 nm/230 THz, and 1550 nm/193 THz). A thorough link budget analysis is conducted to demonstrate the potential of the proposed multi-band architecture for space information networks. Key parameters in the satellite constellation design are investigated to explore the feasibility of deployment at different altitudes in the exosphere orbit (500 km and above). A continuous global coverage is demonstrated to serve the Internet of Space Things, a new paradigm for next generation satellite communication networks. [MTE 4057] Page 3 of 3

The MEC system has two electrodes, cathode and anode, which can either be placed in the same single chamber (single-chamber MEC) or be separately placed in two individual chambers (two-chamber MEC). In the two- chamber MEC, to separate the two chambers, commonly a proton exchange membrane is used. Other recently developed membranes include a charge-mosaic membrane, cation/anion exchange membrane and bipolar membrane. In the two- chamber MEC, the anode chamber is filled with the organic wastewater, while the cathode chamber can be filled with different solutions (like moderate acidified water, phosphate-buffered solution, bicarbonate buffers and salt solution. The main working process in both the MEC types is the same. Electrons get generated by the oxidation of organic matter in the anode, which are transported to the anode. Then, they are transported to the cathode where upon combining with protons, $H$_{2} gets generated. In addition to a potential generated by microorganisms $(- 0.300 V), MEC$ needs a small external potential of more than 0.110 $V$ for the production of $H$_{2}. The external power source use of the battery is generally considered, but the use of renewable power generated from solar, wind, MFCs and waste heat can be seen. questions.question: CASE: The Federal Bureau of Investigation of the $U$.$S$ government, the FBI, was forced to scrap it’s \$170million virtual case file (VCF) management system. Official reports blamed numerous delays, cost overruns, and incompatible software. But a deeper examination of the cause of this failure uncovered issues of control, culture and incompatible organizational systems. Among its many duties, the FBI is charged with the responsibility to fight crime and terrorism. To do so require a large number of agents located within the United States and around the world. That means agents must be able to share information among themselves within the bureau and with other federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies. But sharing information has never been standard operating procedure for this agency. According to one source, ”agents are accustomed to holding information close to their bullet proof vests and scorn the idea of sharing information”. Enter the FBI’s efforts to modernize it’s infrastructure, codenamed “Trilogy”. The efforts included providing agents with 30,000 desktop PC’$s$, high- bandwidth networks to connect FBI locations around the world, and the VCF project to facilitate sharing od case information worldwide. The FBI director explained to congress that VCF would provide “an electronic means for agents to globally send field notes, documents, pieces of intelligence and other evidence so they could hopefully act faster on leads”. It was designed to replace a paper intensive with an electronic web based process. With such a reasonable goals why didn’t it work? The chief information officer (CIO) of the FBI offered one explanation. He claimed that the FBI must radically change the agency culture if the bureau is (HSS 344) Page 2 of 3 ever going to get the high tech analysis and surveillance tools it needs to effectively fight terrorism. We must move from a decentralized amalgam of 56 field offices that are deeply distrustful of technology, outsiders and each other to seamlessly integrated global intelligence operation capable of sharing information and preventing crimes in real-time. A former project manager at the FBI further explained. ”they work under the idea that everything needs to be kept secret. But everything doesn’t have to be kept secret. $T$ do this right, you have to share information.” The VCF system has been shut down, but the CIO is working on a new approach. He is busy trying to win buy in from agents in the field so that the next case management system will work. In addition, he is working to establish a portfolio management plan that will cover all of the FBI’s IT projects, even those begun in decentralized offices. His team has been designing an enterprise architecture that will lay out standards for a bureau wide information system. The director of the FBI has helped too. He reorganized the governance of IT, taking IT budget control away from the districts and giving total IT budget authority to the CIO. The FBI announced that it will build a new case management system called Sentinel in four phases. The new system, according to the CIO, will include workflow, document management, record management, audit trails, access control and single sign-on. To manage the expectations of the agents, the CIO plans to communicate often and significantly increase the training program for the new system. The CIO commented. “we want to automate those things that are most manually cumbersome for the agents so they can see that technology can actually enhance their productivity. That is how to change their attitudes”. Questions: a) What do you think were the real reasons why the VCF system failed? questions.subject: local:management-information-systems
questions.question: CASE: Good Living Pvt. Limited is a sales and service provider for a leading manufacturer of washing machines. In the last three years, the company has sold over 5500 washing machines. Washing machines carry a free on-the-site service arrangement for a period of one year. For the free on-the-site service period of one year, the manufacturer reimburses service charges to Good Living Pvt. Ltd. After the free service period of one year, customer is expected to pay the service charges to Good Living Pvt. Ltd. Typically, customers call up Good Living Pvt. Ltd., showroom or service center and report a problem with their washing machine. Telephone operator notes down the name and address of the customer and the nature of complaint. Service engineers are then deputed to visit the customer’s house to carry out the repairs. When the service engineer visits the customer, the engineer does not have accurate details of date of purchase. As such the engineer is not in a position to decide whether to collect service charges from the customer or whether to claim the service charges from the manufacturer. Many times, service engineers tend to assume that the manufacturer will reimburse service charges and therefore do not insist on customer paying the charges. In the past few months, the number of cases where manufacturer refused to reimburse the service charges has been gradually increasing. The manager observed that the total value of service charges not reimbursed has been Rs. 8000 in last month. The manager therefore instructed the service department to insist on getting the bill number and date of purchase from the customer before a service engineer visits the customer to carry out service on the washing machine. With the date of purchase available, the engineer can be instructed whether to collect service charges from the customer or to claim it from the manufacturer. (HSS 344) Page 2 of 3 This insistence on getting the bill number and date of purchase from the customer was found to create considerable dissatisfaction. When a customer calls to report a complaint, if the telephone operator asks for the date of purchase, many times, customer is unable to give the purchase details such as bill number and date of purchase over the phone. Customers often mention that they have purchased the washing machine “some time back”. In some cases, it was observed that the billing clerk had forgotten to mention the bill details on the warranty card. The customer had the warranty card preserved but not the invoice. Insisting on logging the complaint only after bill number and date is given by the customer was causing delay and was creating considerable customer dissatisfaction. The manager is worried that this customer dissatisfaction may lead to heavy loss of business. At the same time, Good Living Pvt. Ltd. cannot afford to forgo service charges to the extent of Rs. 8000 per month.

questions.question: Case Study: Frederick $W$. Smith and FedEx: In 1965, Yale University undergraduate Frederick $W$. Smith wrote a term paper about the passenger route systems used by most shippers, which he viewed as economically inadequate. Smith wrote of the need for shippers to have an innovative system designed specifically for airfreight that could accommodate time-sensitive shipments such as medicines, computer parts and electronics. His professor gave him a $C$. But he got an A from the marketplace when he launched Federal Express in August 1971. Today FedEx carries 2.1 million envelopes and packages every night; 1.3 million of them arrive at Tennessee alone, where swarms of planes stack up at night waiting to land. Scanners, conveyor belts, workers, delivery trucks, satellite dishes and all form a system that generated \$29.4 billion in sales in 2005 and employs 215,838 workers. Humble beginning:In August of 1971 following a stint in the military, Smith bought controlling interest in Arkansas Aviation Sales, located in Little Rock, Ark. While operating his new firm, Smith identified the tremendous difficulty in getting packages and other airfreight delivered within one to two days. This dilemma motivated him to do the necessary research for resolving the inefficient distribution system. Thus, the idea for Federal Express was born: a company that revolutionized global business practices and now defines speed and reliability. Federal Express was so-named due to the patriotic meaning associated with the word "Federal," which suggested an interest in nationwide economic activity. At that time, Smith hoped to obtain a contract with the Federal Reserve Bank and, although the proposal was denied, he believed the name was a particularly good one for attracting public attention and maintaining name recognition. The company incorporated in June 1971 and officially began operations on April 17, 1973, with the launch of 14 small aircraft from Memphis International Airport. On that night, Federal Express delivered 186 packages to 25 $U$.$S$. cities from Rochester, NY, to Miami, Fla. In the $mid-1970s$, Federal Express took a leading role in lobbying for air cargo deregulation that finally came in 1977. These changes allowed Federal Express to use larger aircraft (such as Boeing $727s$ and McDonnell-Douglas (MME-334.3) Page 2 of 3 $DC-10s)$ and spurred the company's rapid growth. Today FedEx Express has the world's largest all-cargo air fleet, including McDonnell-Douglass $MD-11s$ and Airbus $A-300s$ and $A-310s$. The planes have a total daily lift capacity of more than 26.5 million pounds. In a 24-hour period, the fleet travels nearly 500,000 miles while its couriers $\log$ 2.5 million miles a day - the equivalent of $10^{\wedge 0}$ trips around the earth. FedEx Customer Information Services was established in 2002 as a subsidiary of FedEx Corporate Services, Inc., to align customer contact centers, worldwide revenue operations, claims, $\operatorname{trace}$ and package engineering within FedEx’s professional services company. They had now established an online shipment tracking system wherein the customers could track the status of their shipments online by logging onto the FedEx website and entering the shipment number. Today, FedEx is ranked 214 in the Fortune 500 Global Companies. FedEx Supply Chain Services provides transportation and logistics management, consulting services and other customized supply chain solutions so that customers can maximize potential and minimize costs. Answer the following questions with justification a) As a MIS executive, What type of a Logical Database structure you think (02) would be ideal to track shipments in this case? Justify your answer. $b)$ Mention any 3 advantages that the Online shipment tracking systems have 02) over the conventional tracking system (i.e. calling the office for shipment enquiries$) c)$ Which strategy do you think Frederick $W$. Smith implement which lead to the (02) birth of FedEx? $d)$ What file organization methods support online processing, what are the (02) advantages and limitations of the same and what is the basic distinction between these methods? $e)$ Why is file management important for the overall system performance of an (02) organization? questions.question: Case Study: McDonald’$s$: Using Technology to sell Hamburgers People who think of McDonald's associate it with hamburgers. When they walk into a McDonald'$s$, customers usually do not conclude that it takes a lot of technology to make and sell hamburgers. Until 1980 that was in fact the case. The company followed a traditional path and used computers for basic financial record keeping applications and personnel administration. As long as the monthly books were closed on time and the staffs were paid, people did not place much importance on the role of the technology services group. Today McDonald's is a multinational corporation with 137,000 employees in 68 offices and 14,000 restaurants in 72 countries. There are more than 7,300 restaurants in the United States with \$9 billion in revenue and some 7,000 restaurants overseas with \$3 billion in revenue. McDonald's opens three new stores every 24 hours. Eighty percent of the restaurants are franchised; 20 percent are corporately owned. Based in Oak Brook, Illinois, the \$4 billion dollar company was founded on April 15, 1955. McDonald's is one of the few service companies thriving in the global market. It deals with the international complexity with the following principles: • Put your employees through arduous and repetitive management training. • Form paradigm-busting arrangements with suppliers. • Know a country's culture before you hit the beach. • Hire locals whenever possible. • Maximize autonomy. • Tweak the standard menu only slightly from place to place. • Keep pricing low to build market share; go for economies of scale. Automation of Store Procedures In 1980, Ed Rensi, McDonald's chief operating officer, developed a vision of the strategic role that computers could play in the McDonald's organization. Rensi felt that a tremendous amount of time was spent on paperwork and administrative activity. He asserted that strategic advantage could be achieved through the reduction of the time managers spent counting inventory,' figuring out payroll, or doing a manual crew schedule. Because the rest of the industry was not technology-intensive, anything that could be done to improve efficiency and control costs could be duplicated across all of McDonald's stores, which would lead to substantial increases in the profit margin. Ted Nagengast, a senior systems developer, summarized the focus of the MIS department at McDonald'$s: (MME-334.3)$ Page 2 of 4 McDonald's implemented technology into the restaurant business in four phases. First, the International Business System (lBS) was developed in Europe and Asia. Installed in March 1984, the IBS is now used in approximately one-half of McDonald's overseas restaurants. This system uses IBM midrange computers to get financial jobs done. A key concern in the development of the program was that end users would not be able to change the key business application. According to John Osvath, director of information processing, “We try to insulate the end user from anything outside the application itself." In doing so, McDonald's has avoided on-line, real-time updates of its operations around the world, consolidating its financial reports monthly, as sales figures are reported. Second came the Store Management Business System (SMBS).It managed inventory management, case control, and sales reporting for all of the company-owned restaurants. The In-Store Processor (lSP) was the third step. This system performs cash management, inventorymanagement, and order and crew labor scheduling for the restaurants. One example of the use of this program might be crew labor scheduling. The number of part-time workers that McDonald's employs limits the ability to transmit this information over telephone lines. Through the ISP, relevant data is directly tied to the point-of- sale cash registers. This means that sales, accounting, and inventory updates can be calculated directly from the sales data rather than being manually determined and entered. As a result, three important functions can occur at the same time: • Online link to the point-of-sale register. • Connection to the store manager for information processing. • Link back to corporate headquarters. This system also enables a variety of devices in the store to be connected to the network. Eventually, these will include the point-of-sale register, the time and attendance recorder, security, time reports, and other management items. Communication Technology The fourth installation is the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN). ISDN is a high-speed communication system offered through existing telephone connections. In January 1988, McDonald's corporate headquarters announced that the facility had reached the full power and feature capabilities of ISDN. The company converted all $10^{\wedge 0}$ of the installed telephone lines to AT&$T$'s software. Today, nearly all information and communication systems at McDonald's headquarters in Oak Brook, Illinois, are linked into the ISDN network. This includes mainframes, communications controllers, personal computers, office automation equipment, telephones, and faxes. In all, there are 1,300 digital lines serving 1,110 user stations. In terms of network integration, ISDN allows McDonald's to migrate from existing separate networks to a single, integrated, all-digital network. The primary benefit is the elimination of network confusion through the adoption of a single approach to all communications. This single-network approach will (MME-334.3) Page 3 of 4 control, stabilize, and reduce overall communications expenses. Secondly, using the communication services of the telephone company rather than those of a private system avoids the operational costs and staffing associated with a premise-based switching system. As Carl Dill, vice-president of information services, has stated, "McDonald's does not want to spend money on telecommunications expertise. We want to sell hamburgers." Presently, the tracking and follow-up of proposals is being carried out manually. Mr. Sharma feels that there is room for improvement in the present manual system. He would like an information system to be developed for tracking and follow-up the proposals. The present manual system is described below. As and when a proposal is prepared, it is assigned a reference number. The reference number consists of two sections. The first section or prefix denotes the category of the proposal depending on the type of projects. The second section denotes a running serial number within each category. For example, if the proposal is for consulting services for bridges, the proposal reference number will be prefixed by BRG. If the proposal is for consulting service for railways, the proposal reference number will be prefixed by RLY. The suffix of the reference number is a running serial number within each category. Secretary of Mr. Sharma enters the following details of the proposal in a proposal register. The columns in the proposal register are as follows: Proposal reference number Proposal date Name of the client Brief description of services offered Remarks about follow-up Final decision when order is received Office copies of the proposal are filed in a pending proposal file. When the proposal is converted into an assigned, the office copy of the proposal is removed from the pending proposal file and a new file for the specific assignment is created. questions.question: Case Study: (10) McDonald’$s$: Using Technology to sell Hamburgers People who think of McDonald's associate it with hamburgers. When they walk into a McDonald'$s$, customers usually do not conclude that it takes a lot of technology to make and sell hamburgers. Until 1980 that was in fact the case. The company followed a traditional path and used computers for basic financial record keeping applications and personnel administration. As long as the monthly books were closed on time and the staffs were paid, people did not place much importance on the role of the technology services group. Today McDonald's is a multinational corporation with 137,000 employees in 68 offices and 14,000 restaurants in 72 countries. There are more than 7,300 restaurants in the United States with \$9 billion in revenue and some 7,000 restaurants overseas with \$3 billion in revenue. McDonald's opens three new stores every 24 hours. Eighty percent of the restaurants are franchised; 20 percent are corporately owned. Based in Oak Brook, Illinois, the \$4 billion dollar company was founded on April 15, 1955. McDonald's is one of the few service companies thriving in the global market. It deals with the international complexity with the following principles: • Gather your people often for face-to-face meetings to learn from each other. • Put your employees through arduous and repetitive management training. • Form paradigm-busting arrangements with suppliers. • Know a country's culture before you hit the beach. • Hire locals whenever possible. • Maximize autonomy. • Tweak the standard menu only slightly from place to place. • Keep pricing low to build market share; go for economies of scale. Automation of Store Procedures In 1980, Ed Rensi, McDonald's chief operating officer, developed a vision of the strategic role that computers could play in the McDonald's organization. Rensi felt that a tremendous amount of time was spent on paperwork and administrative activity. He asserted that strategic advantage could be achieved through the reduction of the time managers spent counting inventory,' figuring out payroll, or doing a manual crew schedule. Because the rest of the industry was not technology-intensive, anything that could be done to improve efficiency and control costs could be duplicated across all of McDonald's stores, which would lead to substantial increases in the profit margin. Ted Nagengast, a senior systems developer, summarized the focus of the MIS department at McDonald'$s$: McDonald's implemented technology into the restaurant business in four phases. First, the International Business System (lBS) was developed in Europe and Asia. Installed in March 1984, the IBS is now used in approximately one-half of McDonald's overseas restaurants. (MEE-401.2) Page 2 of 4 This system uses IBM midrange computers to get financial jobs done. A key concern in the development of the program was that end users would not be able to change the key business application. According to John Osvath, director of information processing, “We try to insulate the end user from anything outside the application itself." In doing so, McDonald's has avoided on-line, real-time updates of its operations around the world, consolidating its financial reports monthly, as sales figures are reported. Second came the Store Management Business System (SMBS).It managed inventory management, case control, and sales reporting for all of the company-owned restaurants. The In-Store Processor (lSP) was the third step. This system performs cash management, inventory management, and order and crew labor scheduling for the restaurants. One example of the use of this program might be crew labor scheduling. The number of part-time workers that McDonald's employs limits the ability to transmit this information over telephone lines. Through the ISP, relevant data is directly tied to the point-of-sale cash registers. This means that sales, accounting, and inventory updates can be calculated directly from the sales data rather than being manually determined and entered. As a result, three important functions can occur at the same time: • Online link to the point-of-sale register. • Connection to the store manager for information processing. • Link back to corporate headquarters. This system also enables a variety of devices in the store to be connected to the network. Eventually, these will include the point-of-sale register, the time and attendance recorder, security, time reports, and other management items. Communication Technology The fourth installation is the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN). ISDN is a high-speed communication system offered through existing telephone connections. In January 1988, McDonald's corporate headquarters announced that the facility had reached the full power and feature capabilities of ISDN. The company converted all $10^{\wedge 0}$ of the installed telephone lines to AT&$T$'s software. Today, nearly all information and communication systems at McDonald's headquarters in Oak Brook, Illinois, are linked into the ISDN network. This includes mainframes, communications controllers, personal computers, office automation equipment, telephones, and faxes. In all, there are 1,300 digital lines serving 1,110 user stations. questions.question: Case Study: Frederick $W$. Smith and FedEx: In 1965, Yale University undergraduate Frederick $W$. Smith wrote a term paper about the passenger route systems used by most shippers, which he viewed as economically inadequate. Smith wrote of the need for shippers to have an innovative system designed specifically for airfreight that could accommodate time-sensitive shipments such as medicines, computer parts and electronics. His professor gave him a “$C$”. But he got an A from the marketplace when he launched Federal Express in August 1971. Today FedEx carries 2.1 million envelopes and packages every night; 1.3 million of them arrive at Tennessee alone, where swarms of planes stack up at night waiting to land. Scanners, conveyor belts, workers, delivery trucks, satellite dishes and all form a system that generated \$29.4 billion in sales in 2005 and employs 215,838 workers. Humble beginning: In August of 1971 following a stint in the military, Smith bought controlling interest in Arkansas Aviation Sales, located in Little Rock, Ark. While operating his new firm, Smith identified the tremendous difficulty in getting packages and other airfreight delivered within one to two days. This dilemma motivated him to do the necessary research for resolving the inefficient distribution system. Thus, the idea for Federal Express was born: a company that revolutionized global business practices and now defines speed and reliability. Federal Express was so-named due to the patriotic meaning associated with the word "Federal," which suggested an interest in nationwide economic activity. At that time, Smith hoped to obtain a contract with the Federal Reserve Bank and, although the proposal was denied, he believed the name was a particularly good one for attracting public attention and maintaining name recognition. The company incorporated in June 1971 and officially began operations on April 17, 1973, with the launch of 14 small aircraft from Memphis International Airport. On that night, Federal Express delivered 186 packages to 25 $U$.$S$. Page 2 of 3 cities from Rochester, NY, to Miami, Fla. In the $mid-1970s$, Federal Express took a leading role in lobbying for air cargo deregulation that finally came in 1977. These changes allowed Federal Express to use larger aircraft (such as Boeing $727s$ and McDonnell-Douglas $DC-10s)$ and spurred the company's rapid growth. Today FedEx Express has the world's largest all-cargo air fleet, including McDonnell-Douglass $MD-11s$ and Airbus $A-300s$ and $A-310s$. The planes have a total daily lift capacity of more than 26.5 million pounds. In a 24-hour period, the fleet travels nearly 500,000 miles while its couriers $\log$ 2.5 million miles a day - the equivalent of $10^{\wedge 0}$ trips around the earth. FedEx Customer Information Services was established in 2002 as a subsidiary of FedEx Corporate Services, Inc., to align customer contact centers, worldwide revenue operations, claims, $\operatorname{trace}$ and package engineering within FedEx’s professional services company. They had now established an online shipment tracking system wherein the customers could track the status of their shipments online by logging onto the FedEx website and entering the shipment number. Today, FedEx is ranked 214 in the Fortune 500 Global Companies. FedEx Supply Chain Services provides transportation and logistics management, consulting services and other customized supply chain solutions so that customers can maximize potential and minimize costs.
